description: The Noche Triste, the smallpox epidemic and the siege that ended the Aztec world.
content_html:
The Capture of Moctezuma

When Cortés and his force entered Tenochtitlán in November 1519, they were welcomed as guests but immediately faced a dilemma: they were vastly outnumbered inside a city they could not control. Cortés took a bold decision. Within a week of arrival, he took Moctezuma II hostage, keeping the emperor under Spanish guard while forcing him to continue appearing as ruler. The strategy worked for several months — the Aztec nobility complied with Moctezuma’s instructions, and Cortés used him to demand further tribute and gold.

The situation became unstable in May 1520. While Cortés left Tenochtitlán to deal with a new Spanish expedition sent by Governor Velázquez to arrest him, his deputy Pedro de Alvarado ordered a massacre of Aztec nobles gathered for the festival of Toxcatl. The number killed is debated — Spanish accounts suggest several hundred; some indigenous accounts suggest thousands. The massacre destroyed whatever cooperation the Aztec leadership had extended and triggered a general uprising.

Key Fact

The Toxcatl massacre (May 1520), ordered by Pedro de Alvarado in Cortés’s absence, destroyed Spanish-Aztec cooperation. The subsequent death of Moctezuma (June 1520) — whose exact circumstances remain disputed — removed the last possibility of negotiating through the emperor.

La Noche Triste, June 1520

Moctezuma died in June 1520. Spanish accounts say he was stoned by his own people when he appeared on a balcony to calm the uprising; indigenous accounts suggest the Spanish killed him. Whoever was responsible, his death was catastrophic for the Spanish position. The Aztecs elected a new emperor, Cuitláhuac, who immediately organised a full military assault on the Spanish garrison.

Cortés returned to Tenochtitlán to find his men trapped. On the night of 30 June–1 July 1520, the Spanish and their Tlaxcalan allies attempted to escape the city by night across one of the causeways. The Aztecs discovered the retreat and attacked. The Spanish called this disaster La Noche Triste (“the sad night”). Cortés lost approximately half his Spanish soldiers, most of his horses, and virtually all his artillery and gold. Many men drowned in the lake weighed down by gold they had looted from the treasury.

One of the most decisive factors in the Aztec defeat was not Spanish military superiority but epidemic disease. Smallpox, introduced by a soldier in Velázquez’s expedition (which arrived in 1520), spread through Tenochtitlán and the surrounding population. The indigenous population had no previous exposure to smallpox and therefore no immune resistance — a condition historians call “virgin soil epidemic.” Emperor Cuitláhuac himself died of smallpox within eighty days of taking power. Estimates of Aztec casualties from the 1520 smallpox outbreak range widely, but it clearly devastated the city’s population and military capacity at a critical moment. The disease spread ahead of Spanish armies, weakening peoples before the Spanish even arrived — making it arguably the single most important cause of the conquest.

The Siege of Tenochtitlán, 1521

After La Noche Triste, Cortés retreated to Tlaxcala, where his allies regrouped and resupplied him. He spent the remainder of 1520 rebuilding his force, constructing thirteen armed brigantines (flat-bottomed sailing vessels) for lake warfare, and gathering a vast allied indigenous army. The new Aztec emperor, Cuauhtémoc, had replaced Cuitláhuac (who died of smallpox) and organised a determined defence.

The siege began in May 1521. Cortés’s brigantines took control of the lake, cutting the city’s supply lines. Aztec defenders fought street by street; Cortés systematically demolished buildings to prevent them being reused as strongpoints, gradually reducing the city to rubble. The population suffered from starvation, disease and fighting. On 13 August 1521, Cuauhtémoc attempted to escape by canoe and was captured. The resistance collapsed. The siege had lasted approximately seventy-five days.

Key Fact

Cortés defeated Tenochtitlán through a combination of naval blockade (thirteen brigantines on Lake Texcoco), systematic demolition of the city’s defences, and a vast allied indigenous army — primarily Tlaxcalan — that provided the majority of the fighting force.

The Foundation of Mexico City

The fall of Tenochtitlán on 13 August 1521 ended the Aztec Empire. Cortés ordered the ruins of the city cleared and a new Spanish colonial city built directly on top — an act of deliberate symbolic erasure. Mexico City was constructed on the same island site, reusing Aztec stone and, initially, Aztec labour. The main Spanish cathedral was built on the site of the Templo Mayor — replacing Aztec religious architecture with Christian. This physical overwriting of the Aztec city was a statement about the permanence of Spanish power.

Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521. Cortés initially kept him alive as a useful political figure who could help govern the conquered population. Cuauhtémoc reportedly asked Cortés to kill him rather than live as a prisoner, a request the Spanish did not grant. He was tortured in 1521 to make him reveal the location of hidden Aztec treasure. In 1525, Cortés had him executed, claiming he had discovered a plot against the Spanish. In modern Mexico, Cuauhtémoc is commemorated as a national hero — a symbol of indigenous resistance.
exam_tip_html: For 8-mark “Explain Significance” questions about the fall of the Aztecs, you must address significance both at the time (fall of Tenochtitlán ended the most powerful empire in Mesoamerica; laid the foundations of New Spain) and over time (model for subsequent conquests in the Americas; Columbian Exchange accelerated; millions of indigenous deaths from disease). For 6-mark “Explain a Cause” questions, do not list multiple causes — develop one cause fully with specific evidence, explaining the mechanism, not just the event.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Toxcatl massacre (May 1520) and the disputed death of Moctezuma (June 1520) ended any possibility of Spanish control through the emperor; the Aztecs expelled the Spanish on La Noche Triste (30 June–1 July 1520) with catastrophic losses to Cortés’s force.
  • Smallpox was arguably the decisive factor: introduced in 1520, it killed Emperor Cuitláhuac, devastated the Aztec population and weakened the city’s defences before and during the siege of 1521.
  • The siege of Tenochtitlán (May–August 1521) ended with the capture of the last emperor Cuauhtémoc on 13 August 1521; Cortés built Mexico City on the ruins of the Aztec capital as a statement of permanent Spanish power.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of La Noche Triste (30 June–1 July 1520).
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. the Spanish attempted a night retreat across the causeways / they were attacked by Aztec forces / Cortés lost approximately half his Spanish soldiers, most horses and virtually all his artillery). Two marks for a developed explanation of its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the siege of Tenochtitlán (1521).
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cortés used thirteen armed brigantines on Lake Texcoco to cut the city’s supply lines.
• He systematically demolished buildings to prevent the Aztecs reusing them as defensive strongpoints.
• A large allied indigenous army (primarily Tlaxcalan) provided the majority of the fighting force.
• The last Aztec emperor Cuauhtémoc was captured attempting to escape by canoe on 13 August 1521.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Spanish defeat on La Noche Triste (1520).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the Toxcatl massacre (May 1520) as the cause of the Aztec uprising that trapped the Spanish inside Tenochtitlán; or the death of Moctezuma, which removed the Spanish’s political leverage; explains the causal mechanism fully with specific evidence.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the smallpox epidemic of 1520 for the Aztec defence of Tenochtitlán.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that smallpox killed Emperor Cuitláhuac within eighty days of taking power, creating leadership instability; devastated the Aztec population’s capacity to resist the 1521 siege; indigenous people had no immune resistance to the “virgin soil” epidemic; links specifically to the chronology and evidence.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the fall of Tenochtitlán (1521) for indigenous peoples of central Mexico.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (end of Aztec Empire; Cuauhtémoc captured and eventually executed; Mexico City built on ruins; tribute system replaced by encomienda; Aztec religion suppressed) AND over time (mass depopulation from disease and forced labour; destruction of codices and cultural heritage; Nahua peoples reduced to colonial subjects). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes events without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Disease was the most important reason for the Spanish victory over the Aztec Empire.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Smallpox killed Emperor Cuitláhuac and devastated the population before and during the 1521 siege.
• Indigenous people had no immune resistance; the disease spread ahead of Spanish forces across the Americas.
• The Aztec military capacity was severely weakened at the critical moment of the siege.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Cortés’s alliance with the Tlaxcalans and other anti-Aztec peoples provided the military force that made the siege possible.
• Spanish military technology (steel armour, firearms, horses) gave an advantage in open combat even without disease.
• Internal Aztec divisions and the tribute system’s resentments meant many peoples welcomed or tolerated Spanish rule.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

options: The night Moctezuma was killed by Spanish forces
The night Cortés arrived in Tenochtitlán in November 1519
The disastrous Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlán on the night of 30 June–1 July 1520
The night the Aztecs surrendered to Cortés in August 1521

knowledge_checks.q: Who was the last independent Aztec emperor, captured by the Spanish on 13 August 1521?
Emperor Cuitláhuac died of _____ within eighty days of taking power in 1520.
Cortés built Mexico City directly on the ruins of _____ after 1521.
Match each event to its correct date:

flashcard_questions.q: When was Moctezuma II taken hostage by the Spanish?
flashcard_questions.a: November 1519, within a week of the Spanish arriving in Tenochtitlán.

flashcard_questions.q: What triggered the Aztec uprising against the Spanish in 1520?
flashcard_questions.a: Pedro de Alvarado's massacre of Aztec nobles at the festival of Toxcatl in May 1520.
The disastrous Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlán on the night of 30 June–1 July 1520, when Cortés lost roughly half his men.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did smallpox devastate the Aztec population so severely?
flashcard_questions.a: The indigenous population had no prior exposure and therefore no immune resistance — a 'virgin soil epidemic'.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Aztec emperor died of smallpox within eighty days of taking power?

flashcard_questions.a: The last independent Aztec emperor, who organised the defence of Tenochtitlán in 1521 and was captured on 13 August 1521.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the siege of Tenochtitlán begin?
How did Cortés cut Tenochtitlán's supply lines during the siege?
flashcard_questions.a: Using thirteen armed brigantines to take control of Lake Texcoco.

flashcard_questions.q: On what date did Tenochtitlán fall?
What was built on the ruins of Tenochtitlán after 1521?
flashcard_questions.a: Mexico City, the new capital of New Spain.

flashcard_questions.q: Where was the main Spanish cathedral in Mexico City built?
flashcard_questions.a: On the site of the Templo Mayor — replacing Aztec religious architecture with Christian.

glossary_terms.definition: The ninth Aztec emperor (ruled c.1502–1520) seized by the Spanish inside Tenochtitlán in 1519 and held as a hostage until his death in June 1520.
'The Sad Night' (30 June–1 July 1520): the disastrous Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlán in which Cortés lost approximately half his men, most horses and all his artillery.
Aztec emperor who succeeded Moctezuma in 1520 and organised the expulsion of the Spanish on La Noche Triste; died of smallpox within eighty days of taking power.
The last independent Aztec emperor (ruled 1520–1521) who organised the defence of Tenochtitlán during the 1521 siege and was captured on 13 August 1521.
The Spanish colonial city built on the ruins of Tenochtitlán after 1521, which became the capital of New Spain and is today the capital of Mexico.
